title: Nottingham
description: City and council area in Nottinghamshire, England
wiki_lead:
Nottingham (  NOT-ing-əm) is a city and unitary authority area in Nottinghamshire, East Midlands, England. It is located 42 miles (68 km) south-east of Sheffield and 54 miles (87 km) north-east of Birmingham. Nottingham is the legendary home of Robin Hood's belligerent Sheriff of Nottingham, and is historically associated with the lace-making, bicycle and tobacco industries. The city is also the county town of Nottinghamshire and the settlement was granted its city charter in 1897, as part of Queen Victoria's Diamond Jubilee celebrations. Nottingham is a UNESCO "City of Literature".
In the 2021 census, Nottingham had a reported population of 323,632. The wider conurbation, which includes many of the city's suburbs (including Arnold and Carlton), has a population of 768,638. It is the largest urban area in the East Midlands and the second-largest in the Midlands. Its Functional Urban Area, the largest in the East Midlands, has a population of 919,484. The population of the Nottingham/Derby metropolitan area is estimated to be 1,610,000. The metropolitan economy of Nottingham is the seventh-largest in the United Kingdom with a GDP of $50.9 billion (2014). Aside from Birmingham, it is the only city in the Midlands to be ranked as a sufficiency-level world city by the Globalization and World Cities Research Network.
Nottingham is a major sporting centre and, in October 2015, was named "Home of English Sport". The National Ice Centre, Holme Pierrepont National Water Sports Centre and Trent Bridge international cricket ground are all based in or around the city, which is also the home of two professional football teams: Notts County, recognised as the world's oldest professional league club, and Nottingham Forest, two-time winners of the UEFA European Cup under Brian Clough in 1979 and 1980. The city has professional rugby, ice hockey and cricket teams; it also hosts the Nottingham Open, an international tennis tournament on the ATP and WTA tours. This accolade came just over a year after Nottingham was named as the UK's first City of Football.
The city is served by Nottingham railway station and the Nottingham Express Transit tram system; its bus company, Nottingham City Transport, is the largest publicly owned bus network in England. In December 2015, Nottingham was named a 'City of Literature' by UNESCO, joining a list of 20 Cities of Literature. The title reflects Nottingham's literary heritage, with Lord Byron, D. H. Lawrence and Alan Sillitoe having links to the city, as well as a contemporary literary community, a publishing industry and a poetry scene. The city is served by three universities: the University of Nottingham, Nottingham Trent University and the Nottingham campus of the University of Law; it hosts the highest concentration of higher education providers in the East Midlands.

grok_lead: Nottingham is a city and unitary authority area in Nottinghamshire, England, situated at the heart of the East Midlands region approximately 15 miles northwest of Leicester and 28 miles northeast of Birmingham. Its population stood at 323,700 according to the 2021 census, reflecting a 5.9% increase from 2011 and marking it as one of the more densely populated urban areas in the United Kingdom with around 4,400 residents per square kilometer. The city originated as a Saxon settlement known as Snotingaham in the 6th century, evolving into a medieval stronghold fortified by its natural sandstone caves and cliffs, which facilitated early defensive positions and later underground maltings and tanneries. Historically, Nottingham gained prominence through Nottingham Castle, constructed shortly after the Norman Conquest in 1066 and serving as a royal residence and military outpost, notably during the English Civil War when it was held for the Royalists. The city is indelibly linked to the legendary outlaw Robin Hood, whose tales of resistance against the Sheriff of Nottingham, set against the backdrop of Sherwood Forest to the north, have cemented its cultural identity despite the figure's semi-mythical status rooted in 12th- to 15th-century folklore rather than verifiable history. Nottingham's economy diversified from lace-making and framework knitting in the Industrial Revolution âearning it the moniker "Queen of the Midlands"âto modern strengths in higher education, biomedicine, and advanced manufacturing, bolstered by institutions like Boots, the pharmaceutical giant founded there in 1849, and two Russell Group universities: the University of Nottingham and Nottingham Trent University, which together enroll over 70,000 students. The city's defining characteristics include its extensive network of over 800 man-made caves, used historically for everything from medieval dwellings to Second World War air-raid shelters, and its sporting heritage, particularly football, with Nottingham Forest achieving European Cup victories in 1979 and 1980 under Brian Clough, a feat unmatched by most English clubs. While celebrated for green spaces like the Arboretum and Wollaton Hall âonce home to the deer that inspired the velociraptors in Jurassic Park âNottingham has faced challenges including higher-than-average deprivation indices and crime rates, particularly violent offenses, underscoring urban pressures amid its youthful demographic where nearly 21% of residents are under 18.
